newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish regions see 1997 deficit 27 percent lower.
newsitem.headline: Spanish regions see 1997 deficit 27 percent lower.

text.p: Spain's regional governments plan to shave their non-financial budget deficit by 27 percent in 1997 to a total of 231 billion pesetas, according to a recent publication of the Economy Ministry.

As a ratio over gross domestic product, the regional deficit is seen standing at around 0.3 percent of GDP in 1997 versus 0.43 percent in 1996. GDP is estimated at 77.6 trillion pesetas in 1997 after 73.6 trillion in 1996.
The central government was planning to lower this ratio to 0.2 percent this year, from 0.4 percent in 1996. Last year, the initial deficit ratio forecast was later revised downward.
The Economy Ministry study, published at the end of March, gives the 231 billion peseta figure for the overall regional deficit.
Reuters has calculated the deficit for each individual region based on the study's figures for planned non-financial expenditure and revenue data for this year and last.
The actual deficit of 1996, based on a national account basis, is expected to be published in June or July.

Under a 1996 agreement reached between the central state and the regions, regional governments' 1997 budgets can use 15 percent of Spanish income tax receipts, but must shoulder a bigger share of public expenditures.
As their expenditures rise, the regions will be able to use up to 30 percent of overall Spanish income tax receipts in 1998.
This explain why few regions have an increase in their budget deficit despite increasing expenditures, economists in Madrid said.
For 1997, total expenditures are expected to grow 8.4 percent to 8.86 trillion pesetas, while revenues are seen rising 9.8 percent to 9.8 trillion pesetas.
"That reflects increased importance of regional governments," an economist said.
